title: Ardā Wirāz Nāmag
titleEn: The Book of Arda Viraf — Chapter 1: The Choosing of Wirāz
workEn: The Book of Arda Viraf (Ardā Wirāz Nāmag)
draftNote: The "As written" letters were set down from Haug's printed Pahlavi with the help of his own Roman reading of each word; not every letter has yet been checked against the page.
source: Ardā Wirāz Nāmag, chapter 1, from The Book of Arda Viraf: the Pahlavi text prepared by Destur Hoshangji Jamaspji Asa, revised and collated with further manuscripts by Martin Haug, assisted by E. W. West (Bombay and London, 1872), pp. 3–8, read from the Internet Archive scan (bookofardaviraf00haug). The § numbers are Haug's sentence numbers; later editions divide the chapter differently. Book Pahlavi script has no agreed computer encoding, so the page shows the words as they were read aloud, in D. N. MacKenzie's transcription (the scholarly standard since 1971), and the "As written" switch shows the letters of the script for each word in the usual transliteration, Aramaic word-signs in capitals. The text is Haug's. Where his reading of a word has since been given up, the word is read as it is today and the note says so; where later editors correct the manuscripts, Haug's print is kept and the note gives the correction. Pronunciation: Middle Persian of the third century as MacKenzie reconstructs it. The translation is new, made from the Pahlavi. Still to do: the "As written" letters were set down from Haug's printed Pahlavi with the help of his own Roman reading of each word, and not every letter has yet been checked against the page.
about: The Book of the Righteous Wirāz is the Zoroastrian journey through heaven and hell, often called the Persian Divine Comedy. It was written in Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and took its present form in the ninth or tenth century, from older material. This first chapter sets the scene. Alexander has burned the scriptures and killed the priests, the faith has broken into sects and doubt, and the priests gather at the Farnbāg Fire to send one of their number to the other world to learn whether their rites reach the gods at all. Seven men are picked, then three, then one, Wirāz, who asks only that the choice be confirmed by lot. In the chapters that follow he drinks wine and mang, his soul leaves his body for seven days, and he is shown the rewards of the blessed and the punishments of the damned.

sentences.t: Pad nām ī yazdān.
sentences.l: In the-name of the-gods.
sentences.i: In the name of the gods.
sentences.n: Zoroastrian books open with this formula. yazdān is a plural, 'the divine beings', and came to be used for God. The first three words show how the script works. nām 'name' is written ŠM, the Aramaic word for 'name' (Hebrew שם); pad 'in, at, by' is written with another Aramaic word-sign, PWN; and ī, the little linking word that ties a noun to whatever describes it, is a single stroke. The scribe wrote the Aramaic letters and the reader said the Persian word. Press 'As written' to see every word in the letters of the script: the capitals are word-signs of this kind, the small letters are Persian spelled out.

sentences.t: Ēdōn gōwēnd kū ēw-bār ahlaw Zardušt dēn ī padīrift andar gēhān rawāg be kard.
sentences.l: Thus they-say, that one-time righteous Zardušt the-religion which he-received in the-world current made.
sentences.i: They say that once the righteous Zardušt spread through the world the religion he had received.
sentences.n: The verb waits for the end of its clause, here and throughout: rawāg be kard, 'made current'. be is a small particle set before a verb to mark the act as carried through; you will see it constantly. dēn ī padīrift is 'the religion that he received': ī links a noun to what describes it, here a whole clause. Zardušt is the prophet the Greeks called Zoroaster.

sentences.t: Ud tā bawandagīh ī sēsad sāl dēn andar abēzagīh ud mardōm andar abē-gumānīh būd hēnd.
sentences.l: And until the-completion of three-hundred years the-religion in purity and people in without-doubt-ness were.
sentences.i: And for a full three hundred years the religion stayed pure and people were free of doubt.
sentences.n: būd hēnd is the ordinary past plural, 'they were': būd 'been' with hēnd 'they are'. Both are written with Aramaic word-signs (YHWWN-, HWE-) finished off with Persian endings. abē- is 'without' and -īh makes an abstract noun, so abē-gumān-īh is 'the state of being without doubt'. The three hundred years run from Zardušt to Alexander; the manuscripts write the number in figures.

sentences.t: Ud pas gizistag Gannāg Mēnōg ī druwand, gumān kardan ī mardōmān pad ēn dēn rāy, ān gizistag Aleksandar ī Hrōmāyīg ī Muzrāyīg-mānišn wiyābānēnīd, ī pad garān sezd ud nibard ud dahīg ō Ērān-šahr āmad.
sentences.l: And then the-accursed Foul Spirit, the-wicked, doubt-making of people about this religion for-the-sake-of, that accursed Alexander the Roman, the Egypt-dwelling, led-astray, who with heavy violence and battle and ruin(?) to Iran-realm came.
sentences.i: Then the accursed Evil Spirit, the wicked one, to make people doubt this religion, led astray that accursed Alexander the Roman, who lived in Egypt, and he came against the land of Iran with harsh cruelty, war and ruin.
sentences.n: rāy is a postposition, 'for the sake of', and it governs everything from gumān to dēn: 'for the sake of people's doubting this religion'. Gannāg Mēnōg, the Foul Spirit, is Ahriman, the adversary of Ohrmazd. Alexander is 'Roman' because to Sasanian Persians the Greek-speaking west was the Roman empire; Haug explained 'dwelling in Egypt' by Alexander's having marched on Persia from Egypt. Three words are doubtful. The print spells the name ʾlksgdl, which Haug read Alaksagdar. He read the verb nīyāzānīnīd; it is read today wiyābānēnīd, 'led astray'. And the third of the evils, dahīg in his reading, is a word nobody is sure of: he guessed 'devastation', and the same letters may spell yask, 'sickness'.

sentences.t: U-š ōy Ērān dahibed ōzad, ud dar ud xwadāyīh wišuft ud awērān kard.
sentences.l: And-he that Iran's land-lord killed, and court and lordship wrecked and desolate made.
sentences.i: He killed the ruler of Iran, wrecked the court and the sovereignty, and laid them waste.
sentences.n: u-š is ud 'and' with -š 'he, him, his' attached. Pahlavi hangs its short pronouns on the first word of the clause; u-š and its plural u-šān will come constantly. In a past sentence the attached pronoun is the doer: the grammar says 'and by him the ruler was killed', which English turns into 'he killed'. dahibed is 'lord of the land'; the king meant is Darius III. dar, literally 'door, gate', is the royal court, written BBA, Aramaic bābā 'gate'.

sentences.t: Ud ēn dēn, čiyōn hamāg Abestāg ud Zand, abar gāw pōstīhā ī wirāstag ud pad āb ī zarr nibištag, andar Staxr Pābagān pad diz nibišt nihād ēstād.
sentences.l: And this religion, namely the-whole Avesta and Zand, upon cow skins that (were) prepared and with water of gold written, in Staxr of-Pābag in the-fortress of-writing placed stood.
sentences.i: Now this religion, that is, the whole Avesta and its Zand, written in gold ink on dressed ox-hides, had been deposited at Staxr of Pābag in the Fortress of Archives.
sentences.n: The Avesta is the scripture, in its own ancient language; the Zand is its translation and commentary in Pahlavi. Staxr, beside the ruins of Persepolis, was the home city of the Sasanian house, whose ancestor was Pābag. nihād ēstād, 'stood placed', is how Pahlavi says 'had been placed'. āb ī zarr, 'water of gold', is gold ink. Four word-signs here will be familiar from Hebrew: āb 'water' is written MYA (מים), zarr 'gold' ZHBA (זהב), gāw 'cow' TWRA (Aramaic tōrā, Hebrew שור), and diz 'fortress' KLYTA, Aramaic for 'town' (Hebrew קריה). Whether diz nibišt names a building, the 'fortress of writings', or simply means 'the archives' is not settled.

sentences.t: Ud ōy petyārag ī wad-baxt ī ahlomōγ ī druwand ī anāg-kardār Aleksandar ī Hrōmāyīg ī Muzrāyīg-mānišn abar āwurd ud be sōxt.
sentences.l: And that adversary, the ill-fated, the heretic, the wicked, the evil-doer Alexander the Roman, the Egypt-dwelling, carried (it) off and burned (it).
sentences.i: That ill-starred adversary, the heretic, the wicked evil-doer Alexander the Roman, who lived in Egypt, carried it off and burned it.
sentences.n: A string of epithets, each hooked on with ī, before the name arrives. ahlomōγ is the standing word for a heretic or false teacher. The memory of Alexander burning the scriptures runs through Zoroastrian tradition; Greek writers record that he burned the palace at Persepolis.

sentences.t: Ud čand dastwarān ud dādwarān ud hērbedān ud mowbedān ud dēn-burdārān ud abzārōmandān ud dānāgān ī Ērān-šahr rāy be kušt.
sentences.l: And several high-priests and judges and teacher-priests and chief-priests and religion-bearers and capable-ones and wise-ones of Iran-realm he-killed.
sentences.i: He killed a good many of the high priests and judges, the teaching priests and chief priests, the upholders of the religion, and the able and the learned of the land of Iran.
sentences.n: rāy here marks the direct object, the people killed; that is a different job from the 'for the sake of' of §3. The titles are grades of the priesthood: the dastwar, the authority on doctrine (the Parsi 'dastur'); the hērbed, the teaching priest; the mowbed, 'chief of the magi'.

sentences.t: Ud mehān ud kadag-xwadāyān ī Ērān-šahr ēk abāg did kēn ud anāštīh ō mayān abgand, ud xwad škast, ō dušox dwārist.
sentences.l: And the-great-ones and house-lords of Iran-realm, one with the-other, hatred and un-peace into the-midst he-threw, and himself broke, to hell scuttled.
sentences.i: He sowed hatred and strife among the nobles and the heads of households of Iran, setting one against another; then he himself was broken and went headlong to hell.
sentences.n: ēk abāg did, 'one with another', is the set phrase for 'each other'. dwārist is one of the verbs Zoroastrian texts keep for evil beings: good creatures 'go', demons and the wicked 'scuttle'. Pahlavi has a whole second vocabulary of this kind. xwad škast, 'himself broke', is taken to mean Alexander's early death.

sentences.t: Ud pas az ān mardōmān ī Ērān-šahr ēk abāg did āšōb ud pahikār būd.
sentences.l: And after that, the-people of Iran-realm, one with the-other, turmoil and quarrel there-was.
sentences.i: After that the people of Iran fell into turmoil and quarrelling among themselves.
sentences.n: Here 'people' is spelled out in Persian letters (mltwmʾn). In §2 the same word was written with the Aramaic word-sign ANŠWTA (Aramaic אנשא, Hebrew אנוש). A scribe could do either.

sentences.t: Ud čiyōn-išān xwadāy ud dahibed ud sālār ud dastwar ī dēn-āgāh nē būd, ud pad tis ī yazdān gumān būd hēnd.
sentences.l: And as to-them lord and land-lord and chief and high-priest who (was) religion-knowing not there-was, and about the-matter of the-gods doubting they-were.
sentences.i: And since they had no lord, no ruler, no chief and no high priest versed in the religion, they came to doubt the things of God.
sentences.n: čiyōn-išān is čiyōn 'as, since' with -išān 'them' attached. Having is said with 'to': 'to them there was no lord'. tis 'thing, matter' is written MNDOM, Aramaic for 'something' (מנדעם).

sentences.t: Ud was ēwēnag kēš ud wurrōyišn, ǰud-ristagīh ud gumānīh ud ǰud-dādestānīh andar gēhān be ō paydāgīh āmad.
sentences.l: And many kinds (of) creed and belief, separate-sect-ness and doubting and separate-judgment-ness in the-world forth to appearance came.
sentences.i: Creeds and beliefs of many kinds, sects, doubt and conflicting rulings came into the open in the world.
sentences.n: ǰud- 'apart, different' builds the words for heresy: ǰud-ristagīh 'being of a separate sect', ǰud-dādestānīh 'disagreement in judgment'. ō paydāgīh āmad, 'came to visibility', is the idiom for 'appeared'.

sentences.t: Tā ān ka zād hu-fraward anōšag-ruwān Ādurbād ī Māraspandān, kē padiš, pad sāxt ī pad dēn kard, rōy ī widāxtag abar war rēxt.
sentences.l: Until that (time) when was-born the-blessed immortal-souled Ādurbād son-of-Māraspand, who, upon him, in the-trial(?) which by the-religion was-made, brass that (was) molten upon the-breast was-poured.
sentences.i: So it went until the birth of the blessed Ādurbād son of Māraspand, of immortal soul, on whose breast molten brass was poured in the ordeal held according to the religion.
sentences.n: Ādurbād was high priest under Shapur II (309–379). Tradition says that to prove the true doctrine against the sects he had molten metal poured on his chest and rose unharmed. hu-fraward and anōšag-ruwān, 'of immortal soul', are what one says of the honoured dead. The middle of the sentence is doubtful. Haug's print has pad sāxt ī pad dēn kard, and he translated 'in the tale which is in the Dēnkard', taking dēn kard as the title of a book. Editors since read the first two words as one, passāxt 'ordeal', and that is the sense given here.

sentences.t: Ud čand dādestān ud dādwarīh abāg ǰud-kēšān ud ǰud-wurrōyišnān be kard.
sentences.l: And several judgments and adjudications with the-separate-creed-ones and separate-belief-ones he-made.
sentences.i: And he argued and judged many a case against the sectarians and those of other beliefs.
sentences.n: dādestān covers 'judgment, case, legal opinion'. The disputations of Ādurbād with the heretics are meant.

sentences.t: Ud ēn dēn andar Šaspīgān, mardōmān andar gumān būd hēnd.
sentences.l: And this religion in the-Šaspīgān(?), the-people in doubt were.
sentences.i: And this religion was in the Šaspīgān(?), and the people were in doubt.
sentences.n: A doubtful sentence. Haug's print reads Šaspīgān, a name the Dēnkard gives to the royal treasury where a copy of the scripture was kept. Later editors correct the word to šēbišn, 'agitation', and add an 'and' after it: 'this religion was in turmoil and people were in doubt', which fits the story better.

sentences.t: Ud pas moγ-mardān ud dastwarān ī dēn any būd hēnd; az ān mar xwadāy-ōmand ud purr-pīm būd hēnd.
sentences.l: And then magus-men and high-priests of the-religion, other-ones, there-were; of that number (they) lord-having(?) and full-of-grief were.
sentences.i: Later there were other magi and high priests of the religion, and they among that number were loyal(?) and full of grief.
sentences.n: moγ-mard, 'magus-man', is a Zoroastrian priest; this is the word behind the Magi. The second half is uncertain. Haug's print has xwadāy-ōmand, 'having a lord', which he took as 'loyal', with az ān mar as 'out of that number'. Editors since read andōhōmand, 'sorrowful', and take az ān mar as 'on that account': 'at this they were troubled and full of grief'.

sentences.t: U-šān pad dar ī pērōzgar Ādur ī Farnbāg hanǰaman xwāst.
sentences.l: And-they at the-court of the-victorious Fire that (is) Farnbāg an-assembly called-for.
sentences.i: They called an assembly at the court of the victorious Farnbāg Fire.
sentences.n: Ādur Farnbāg was one of the three great sacred fires of Sasanian Iran, the fire of the priestly estate. 'Victorious' is the standing epithet of a consecrated fire. Haug read the name Frōbāg.

sentences.t: Ud was ēwēnag saxwan ud uskār abar ēn būd, kū-mān čārag xwāstan abāyēd,
sentences.l: And many kinds (of) speech and deliberation upon this there-were, that: for-us a-remedy to-seek is-necessary,
sentences.i: There was much talk and deliberation of every kind on this point: "We must look for a way,
sentences.n: From here to §27 the assembly speaks. kū 'that' opens reported speech and does the work of a quotation mark. kū-mān is kū with -mān 'us' attached; abāyēd 'it is necessary' takes the infinitive: 'for us to seek a remedy is necessary'. saxwan 'word, speech' is written MRYA, Aramaic for 'word' (Hebrew מלה; the script writes L and R with one letter).

sentences.t: tā-mān kas-ē šawēd ud az mēnōgān āgāhīh āwarēd,
sentences.l: so-that of-us some one may-go and from the-spirit-beings knowledge may-bring,
sentences.i: so that one of us may go and bring back word from the spirit world,
sentences.n: kas-ē is 'some one person': kas 'person' with -ē 'a, one', which the scribe writes as the figure 1. kas itself is written AYŠ, the Hebrew איש. mēnōg is the unseen, spiritual state of existence, set against gētīg, the world of matter; the mēnōgān are the beings of that state.

sentences.t: kū mardōmān ī andar ēn āwām hēnd be dānēnd kū ēn yazišn ud drōn ud āfrīnagān ud nērang ud pādyābīh ud yōǰdahrīh ī amā pad kardag āwarēm ō yazdān rasēd ayāb ō dēwān,
sentences.l: that the-people who in this age are may-know whether this worship and sacred-bread and blessings and ritual-formula and ablution and purification which we into practice bring to the-gods arrives or to the-demons,
sentences.i: so that the people of this age may know whether the worship, the offering of sacred bread, the blessings, the ritual formulas, the ablutions and the purifications that we perform reach the gods or the demons,
sentences.n: A list of the main rites: the yazišn (the Yasna, the daily liturgy), the drōn (the consecrated flat bread and its service), the āfrīnagān (ceremonies of blessing), nērang (ritual formulas), pādyābīh (ritual washing). pad kardag āwurdan, 'to bring into practice', is 'to perform'. dēw 'demon' is written ŠDYA, Aramaic šēdā (Hebrew שד). The fear behind the question is a real one in Zoroastrian thinking: a rite done wrongly feeds the demons.

sentences.t: ud ō frayād ī ruwān ī amā rasēd ayāb nē.
sentences.l: and to the-aid of the-soul of us arrives or not.
sentences.i: and whether or not they come to the help of our souls."

sentences.t: U-šān pas pad ham-dādestānīh ī az dēn dastwarān hamāg mardōm ō dar ī Ādur Farnbāg xwand hēnd.
sentences.l: And-by-them then, with the-agreement that (came) from the-religion's high-priests, all the-people to the-court of the-Fire Farnbāg were-called.
sentences.i: Then, with the agreement of the high priests of the religion, they summoned all the people to the court of the Farnbāg Fire.
sentences.n: xwand hēnd is 'were called', a passive: the people are the subject and u-šān at the head of the sentence names the callers, 'by them'. ham-dādestānīh is 'being of the same judgment', agreement.

sentences.t: U-šān az hamōyēn ǰudāg kard haft mard kē pad yazdān ud dēn abē-gumāntar būd hēnd,
sentences.l: And-they from the-whole apart made seven men who about the-gods and the-religion more-without-doubt were,
sentences.i: And from all of them they set apart seven men who were the surest in their faith in the gods and the religion,
sentences.n: -tar is the 'more' ending, like English -er; with nothing to compare against it means 'most of all'. haft 'seven' is written here as a figure. mard 'man' is GBRA, Aramaic gabrā (Hebrew גבר), and kē 'who' is MNW, Aramaic mannū, 'who is it' (מן הוא).

sentences.t: u-šān xwēš menišn ud gōwišn ud kunišn wirāstagtar ud frārōntar,
sentences.l: and-their own thought and speech and deed (were) more-ordered and more-upright,
sentences.i: and whose own thoughts, words and deeds were the best ordered and the most upright;
sentences.n: Thought, word and deed (menišn, gōwišn, kunišn) are the three measures of a person in Zoroastrian ethics; they return at the end of the chapter. -išn makes a noun from a verb's present stem. xwēš 'own' is written NPŠE, Aramaic nafšeh 'his self' (Hebrew נפש).

sentences.t: ud guft kū ašmā xwēšīhā be nišīnēd, ud az ašmā ēk-ē kē pad ēn kār weh ud awināhtar ud husrawtar be wizīnēd.
sentences.l: and (they) said that: you by-yourselves sit-down, and from you one who for this task (is) better and more-sinless and of-better-fame choose.
sentences.i: and they said to them, "Sit down among yourselves, and choose the one of you who is best for this task, the most blameless and of the best name."
sentences.n: nišīnēd and wizīnēd are commands to several people. -īhā makes an adverb: xwēšīhā, 'in your own way, by yourselves'. ašmā 'you' is written LKWM, Aramaic 'to you' (לכם), and weh 'good, better' is ŠPYL, Aramaic šappīr 'fine, good' (שפיר).

sentences.t: Ud pas awēšān haft mard be nišast hēnd,
sentences.l: And then those seven men sat-down,

sentences.t: ud az haft sē ud az sē ēk-ē, Wirāz nām, be wizīd; ud ast kē Nēšāpūr nām gōwēnd.
sentences.l: and from the-seven three, and from the-three one, Wirāz by-name, (they) chose; and there-is who Nēšāpūr by-name call (him).
sentences.i: and out of the seven they chose three, and out of the three one, Wirāz by name; some call him Nēšāpūr.
sentences.n: The hero's name. Its last letter can be read z or p (and p also stands for f). The Parsi tradition read Vīrāf, Haug followed it, and the book is still best known as the Book of Arda Viraf. The Avesta has a name Virāza, and Wirāz is the reading usual today. ardā, 'righteous', the title he carries in the rest of the book, is an older form of the word ahlaw in §1. ast kē, 'there is who', means 'some people'. Whether Nēšāpūr is a second name or means 'the man from Nishapur' is not known.

sentences.t: Ud pas ōy Wirāz, čiyōn-iš ān saxwan ašnūd, abar ō pāy ēstād, ud dast pad kaš kard ud guft
sentences.l: And then that Wirāz, as-he that speech heard, up onto foot stood, and hand in armpit put and said
sentences.i: Then Wirāz, when he heard what was said, rose to his feet, folded his arms across his chest and said,
sentences.n: dast pad kaš kardan, 'to put the hands in the armpits', is the posture of respect before a superior: arms folded, hands tucked away. pāy 'foot' is written LGLE (Hebrew רגל) and dast 'hand' YDE (Hebrew יד). saxwan is spelled out in Persian letters here; in §22 it was the word-sign MRYA.

sentences.t: kū agar-tān sahēd ēg-im akāmagōmand mang ma dahēd, tā ašmā māzdēsnān ud man nāhīčag abganēd,
sentences.l: that: if-to-you it-seems (good), then-to-me, unwilling, mang do-not give, until you Mazda-worshippers and I the-lot cast,
sentences.i: "If it please you, do not give me the mang against my will until you, Mazda-worshippers, have cast lots between yourselves and me.
sentences.n: mang is the drug Wirāz will drink in wine in the next chapter to send his soul out of his body; it is usually taken to be henbane or hemp. māzdēsn, 'Mazda-worshipper', is the Zoroastrians' own name for themselves. ma is the 'not' used with commands, written AL (Hebrew אל). man 'I, me' is written with the single letter L, Aramaic 'to me' (לי). The word for the lot, nāhīčag in Haug's reading, is rare and its exact form is uncertain.

sentences.t: ud agar nāhīčag ō man rasēd, kāmagōmandīhā šawam ō ān gyāg ī ahlawān ud druwandān, ud ēn paygām drustīhā baram ud rāstīhā āwaram.
sentences.l: and if the-lot to me arrives, willingly I-go to that place of the-righteous and the-wicked, and this message soundly I-carry and truly I-bring.
sentences.i: If the lot falls to me, I will go willingly to that place of the righteous and the wicked, and I will carry this message faithfully and bring back a true answer."
sentences.n: šawam, baram, āwaram are plain presents, 'I go, I carry, I bring'; Pahlavi uses the present for a promise. The place of the righteous and the wicked is the other world, heaven and hell, which the rest of the book describes.

sentences.t: Ud pas awēšān māzdēsnān ud man nāhīčag āwurd: fradom bār pad humat, ud dudīgar bār pad hūxt, ud sidīgar bār pad huwaršt; harw sē nāhīčag ō Wirāz āmad.
sentences.l: And then (for) those Mazda-worshippers and me the-lot (they) brought: the-first time with good-thought, and the-second time with good-word, and the-third time with good-deed; every three lots to Wirāz came.
sentences.i: Then the lots were cast for those Mazda-worshippers and me: the first time for Good Thought, the second for Good Word, the third for Good Deed. All three lots fell to Wirāz.
sentences.n: 'And me': for two words the telling slips into Wirāz's own voice; not all of Haug's manuscripts have them. humat, hūxt, huwaršt, 'well thought, well said, well done', are the Avesta's own words for the three-part ethic, kept in their old form. harw sē, 'every three', is 'all three'.
